text:
Let Drivers Pay for Their Own Parking

Walk through almost any American city and you will find a quiet rule shaping the ground beneath your feet. Before a developer can build an apartment block, a corner restaurant, or a small clinic, the city usually demands a fixed number of parking spaces. Two per home. One for every few hundred square feet of retail. One for every few seats in a dining room. These minimum parking requirements are rarely debated in public, yet they may be the most expensive planning rule most residents have never heard of. Cities should repeal them.

Start with the numbers that planners themselves cannot defend. Parking minimums were not derived from careful study of what people need. Many were borrowed from other cities, or based on the peak demand measured at a handful of suburban sites, often with free parking on offer. Donald Shoup, the economist who spent decades studying the subject, showed that the standard manuals rest on thin and wildly variable data. A rule built on guesses, enforced as law, produces predictable errors. We end up with lots sized for the busiest shopping day of the year that sit mostly empty the other three hundred and sixty four.

Those empty spaces are not free. Structured parking can cost tens of thousands of dollars per space to build, and underground parking costs far more. Surface lots are cheaper to build but swallow land that could hold homes or shops. Either way the cost lands somewhere. It is folded into rents, menu prices, and purchase prices, and it is paid by everyone, including the household that owns no car. A family that cannot afford a vehicle ends up subsidizing the storage of other people's vehicles every time they rent an apartment. That is a regressive tax hidden inside a zoning code.

The effect on housing is where the rule does its worst damage. When a city requires two spaces per unit, a small lot that could hold eight modest apartments may only fit five once the parking is accounted for. Sometimes the project simply dies, because the math stops working. Developers respond by building fewer, larger, pricier units, since the parking cost is the same whether the apartment is tiny or generous. In cities with severe shortages, this is an absurd trade. We are protecting vehicle storage at the expense of human shelter.

Then there is the damage to places themselves. Cities that mandate parking spread buildings apart, because every destination needs its moat of asphalt. Walking from one shop to the next becomes unpleasant or pointless, so people drive even for short trips, which in turn seems to justify the parking. Historic main streets, with their tight rows of shops built before the mandates arrived, are often illegal to build today. Many older neighborhoods that people love and pay a premium to live in could not be built under current rules. That should tell us something.

Critics raise a fair worry. If cities stop requiring parking, will streets overflow with cars and neighbors fight over curb space? Consider what repeal actually does. It does not ban parking. It removes the mandate and lets the builder and the market decide. A suburban office park or a grocery store will still provide plenty, because customers expect it. A downtown apartment near transit may provide less, because the tenants it attracts own fewer cars. Lenders and developers have strong incentives to build what their tenants will use. The real change is that the decision moves from a rulebook to the people who are spending the money and bearing the risk.

Where spillover does become a problem, there are better tools than mandates. Cities can price curb parking sensibly, issue permits for residents, and share the revenue with the neighborhood so that people see a benefit. Buffalo became the first major American city to eliminate citywide minimums in 2017, and others including Minneapolis, Austin, and a growing list of smaller places have followed with broad reforms. The sky did not fall. Developers kept building parking where it made sense, and projects that were once impossible began to pencil out.

There is also a climate and budget argument. Cities that invite more driving by design take on the costs of wider roads, longer utility lines, and more stormwater runoff from paved surfaces. Compact development, which parking mandates discourage, tends to be cheaper to serve and kinder to the environment. Repealing the rule nudges growth in a healthier direction without a single new subsidy.

Nothing here requires believing that cars are evil or that everyone should give them up. Most people will keep driving, and good businesses will keep serving them. The argument is narrower and stronger than that. A city should not force every building to subsidize driving whether or not its users want it. Let owners weigh the cost of a space against the value of a tenant or a customer. Let neighborhoods manage the curb honestly with prices rather than guesses. Some projects will include lots of parking and some will include almost none, and both outcomes will be better than a single number written decades ago by someone who never saw the site.

Repeal minimum parking requirements. Trust builders, buyers, and residents to decide how much pavement they actually need.
